extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students studying representation theory and quantum computation
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and problem set on characters of finite groups (definitions, orthogonality, character tables, Frobenius divisibility, Burnside, Frobenius determinant) with examples and exercises. Focused on computing and using characters to decompose representations and deduce group-theoretic facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear independence of irreducible characters
rubrics_metrics.description: If χV1, …, χVr are characters of distinct irreducible representations, then any linear relation c1χV1 + ··· + crχVr = 0 (as class functions) implies c1 = ··· = cr = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduce from the density theorem / structure A = ⊕i Mat(Vi) and the fact that each Mat(Vi) has one-dimensional abelianization; the linear independence can also be checked by pairing with appropriate matrix units. (See Question 21.2.6 and surrounding discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of irreps equals number of conjugacy classes
rubrics_metrics.description: For a finite group G, the number r of irreducible complex representations equals the number of conjugacy classes of G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows because characters of irreps form a basis of the space of class functions Funclass(G), whose dimension is the number of conjugacy classes. Use the earlier linear independence result and the count dim(A/[A,A]) = r.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner product on class functions (Funclass(G))
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ⟨f1,f2⟩ = (1/|G|) Σ_{g∈G} f1(g) f2(g) for class functions f1,f2: Classes(G) → C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inner product (dot product) is used to express orthogonality relations of characters and to compute multiplicities of irreps inside representations; it is the primary computational tool for character table work (see examples and exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonality theorem for characters
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite-dimensional complex representations V and W of G, ⟨χV, χW⟩ = dim Hom_rep(W, V). In particular, for irreps V and W, ⟨χV, χW⟩ = 1 if V ≅ W and 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses dual and tensor representations to reduce ⟨χV,χW⟩ to the trace of the averaging projector P = (1/|G|)Σ_g g acting on V⊗W^∨; im P is the space of G-intertwiners. Consequence: characters of irreps form an orthonormal basis of Funclass(G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character trace identities (direct sum, tensor, dual)
rubrics_metrics.description: If V and W are finite-dimensional representations then (a) χ_{V⊕W}(g) = χ_V(g) + χ_W(g), (b) χ_{V⊗W}(g) = χ_V(g)·χ_W(g), and (c) χ_{V^∨}(g) = χ_V(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parts (a) and (b) follow from trace identities Tr(S⊕T)=Tr(S)+Tr(T) and Tr(S⊗T)=Tr(S)Tr(T). For (c) diagonalize ρ(g) and use eigenvalues being roots of unity (so λ^{-1}=conjugate). Warning: (b) and (c) do not extend linearly to C[G] (see Remark 21.3.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for irreducibility via inner product
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite-dimensional representation V is irreducible iff ⟨χ_V, χ_V⟩ = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute character values χ_V(g) for each g and check the inner product norm. Examples: use the S3 and S4 character tables to verify irreducibility numerically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading decompositions from characters (multiplicity formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: If V1,…,Vr are the irreps of G and W is any complex representation, then the multiplicity n_i of Vi in W is n_i = ⟨χ_W, χ_{Vi}⟩ and W ≅ ⊕_{i=1}^r Vi^{⊕ n_i}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 21A: prove each n_i is a non-negative integer and reconstruct W from character inner products; this is the standard way to decompose representations once you know the character table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second orthogonality formula (columns orthogonality)
rubrics_metrics.description: For g,h ∈ G and irreps V1,…,Vr, Σ_{i=1}^r χ_{Vi}(g) χ_{Vi}(h) = 0 unless g and h are conjugate, in which case the sum equals |C_G(g)| (up to normalization as stated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement appears as Problem 21E⋆. This column orthogonality is the complementary orthogonality relation used to deduce conjugacy/class-size information from characters (useful in proofs like Lemma 22.2.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using orthogonality and dimension constraints to compute character tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute unknown character table entries by using: (i) orthonormality relations, (ii) sum of squares of dimensions equals |G|, (iii) known one-dimensional characters (trivial and sign), and (iv) tensoring with one-dimensional characters to obtain other rows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked examples: D10 and S4: determine possible irreducible dimensions from the sum of squares, compute traces (e.g., reflection representation), use norms ⟨χ,χ⟩=1 and orthogonality to fill remaining rows; tensoring with sign preserves norms (see S4 example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: elements of Z[G] are integral
rubrics_metrics.description: If α ∈ Z[G], then α is integral over Z: there exists a monic polynomial with integer coefficients P such that P(α) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Noetherian property of Z[G] and finite generation of the Z-span of powers of α (see Lemma 22.1.2). This lemma is used in algebraic-integer arguments like Frobenius divisibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frobenius divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If V is a complex irreducible representation of finite group G, then dim V divides |G|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: show |G|/dim V is an algebraic integer by expressing it as |G|⟨χ_V,χ_V⟩/dim V and splitting sums over conjugacy classes; use that certain traces are algebraic integers (Schur's lemma and previous lemma) and χ_V(Ci) are sums of roots of unity. See Theorem 22.1.1 and its proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: gcd(|C|, dim V)=1 implies scalar action or zero trace
rubrics_metrics.description: If V is an irreducible complex representation and C is a conjugacy class with gcd(|C|, dim V)=1, then for g∈C either ρ(g) is scalar or χ_V(g)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From algebraic-number arguments: |C|·χ_V(g)/dim V ∈ Z (from Frobenius argument), so if gcd(|C|,n)=1 then χ_V(g)/n ∈ Z which forces either all eigenvalues equal (scalar) or sum zero. This lemma is Lemma 22.2.2 and is used in Burnside's argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple groups cannot have prime-power conjugacy classes
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite simple group cannot have a conjugacy class whose size is a nontrivial prime power p^k (k>0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction uses the second orthogonality formula, existence of a nontrivial irrep with p ∤ dim V and nonzero χ_V(g) (Exercise 22.2.4), and then constructs a nontrivial normal subgroup from commutators of class elements acting trivially in that irrep (see Lemma 22.2.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burnside's pa q b theorem (non-simplicity of groups of order p^a q^b)
rubrics_metrics.description: If |G| = p^a q^b for distinct primes p,q (a,b ≥ 0) and G is nonabelian, then G is not simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partition group into conjugacy classes: classes are size 1 or divisible by pq; deduce center must be nontrivial, giving a nontrivial normal subgroup, contradicting simplicity. Uses Lemma 22.2.3 and earlier orthogonality tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frobenius determinant factorization theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: For the |G|×|G| matrix M_G with variables x_g at entry (g,h) = x_{gh}, det M_G factors over C into irreducible polynomials such that (i) the number of irreducible factors equals the number of conjugacy classes of G, and (ii) the multiplicity of each irreducible polynomial equals its degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the regular representation Reg(C[G]) decomposed as ⊕_i V_i^{⊕ dim V_i}; the determinant of the generic linear map T decomposes as ∏_i (det T|_{V_i})^{dim V_i}. Show each det(T|_{V_i}) is irreducible (density theorem gives generic surjectivity to all matrices) and distinct; recover characters from coefficients of these polynomials (Exercise 22.3.3). Examples: Z/2Z and S3 factorization illustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density theorem / generic surjectivity consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: For an irreducible representation V_i, the map from coefficients {x_g} to linear combinations Σ_g x_g ρ_i(g) can achieve any matrix in Mat(V_i); thus the entries of the generic matrix are linearly independent polynomial variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the irreducibility of the Frobenius determinant factors: a linear change of variables reduces to determinant of a generic matrix (which is irreducible). This is an application of the density theorem mentioned throughout the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tensoring by one-dimensional representations preserves irreducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If V and W are irreps with dim W = 1, then V⊗W is irreducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 21C: since one-dimensional characters are homomorphisms G→C^×, tensoring by them twists representations but doesn't introduce nontrivial invariant subspaces; can be seen via characters and inner product norms.
